blocks.text: 在 Anthropic，AI 如何重构了工作与就业？作为处于 AI 应用前沿的公司，Anthropic 可能是 AI 将如何改变整个经济中的工作组织、招聘和劳动力需求的一个领先指标。

inlines.text: 在 Anthropic，AI 如何重构了工作与就业？作为处于 AI 应用前沿的公司，Anthropic 可能是 AI 将如何改变整个经济中的工作组织、招聘和劳动力需求的一个领先指标。

blocks.text: 主要发现

inlines.text: 主要发现
Anthropic 招聘的初级技术岗位占比一直在缩小。与此同时，AI 智能体相对于员工的工作时长迅速扩大。到 8 月，交互式 AI 智能体的工作时长以 6 比 1 超过员工。
随着 AI 智能体在公司内扩散，Anthropic 开始实现人均产出更多代码、每位销售代表完成更多销售、处理更多合同。对同一员工进行长期追踪，随着他们采用新的 AI 工具，产出随之上升。
这种加速使人类注意力成为智能体产出的瓶颈。即使在非技术员工中，阅读其 Claude 智能体的全部输出也会占用他们半个工作周。作为应对，员工转向“元工作”，即构建可见性工具和监控智能体流水线。
工作组织的变化反映在招聘经理不断变化的优先事项上，他们越来越强调自主性和判断力，而非技术领域专长和具体执行。

blocks.text: 在 AI 日益强大的背景下，我们可以预期工作与就业会发生哪些转变？Anthropic 值得研究，因为它已围绕 AI 彻底重塑了自身的工作流程。智能体在 Slack 聊天中穿梭并安排会议。它们自主修复漏洞，并集体攻克庞大的工程项目。智能体工作时长以 6 比 1 超过人类工时。Anthropic 当下正在发生的变化，为未来工作与就业的可能图景提供了超前信号。

blocks.text: 我们发现，即使公司不断增长，初级技术岗位的相对招聘也已放缓。工程师和非技术员工的生产率都大幅跃升，且在他们采用编码智能体时提升尤为明显。招聘经理越来越强调应聘者的自主性和判断力，而非具体技术专长。在 AI 密集型组织中工作的一个决定性特征，是持续面临尽可能把自己从这一瓶颈位置精简出去的压力。一位工程师将工作描述为面对“一支 Claude 大军，每一个都在要求我的关注”。Anthropic 的员工仍持批判态度。但他们贡献的性质已经改变。

blocks.text: 与此同时，Anthropic 内部技术部门的整体就业占比在过去一年从 61% 降至 56%。随着公司扩张，技术招聘的绝对数量仍在持续增长，但销售、财务和招聘方面的大规模招聘增速更快。这一变化部分源于公司规模扩大时业务职能的自然扩张。部分也可能反映出编码工具日益让非技术员工能够自己开发软件。例如，一位销售代表为自己工作量身定制了一个仪表盘和销售管道：“这种搭建本来超出我的能力范围，尤其是 UI、连接所有工具、MCP 这些。但我大概花了三四个小时就做出来了，就是不断迭代。”非技术员工（定义为基线时没有代码提交的人，不含新员工）以编码为重点的 AI 代理会话从 2025 年 8 月的每月 2 次跃升至 2026 年 5 月的 90 次。

blocks.text: 然而，这种招聘构成的变化并不仅仅是自动化编码向 其他领域专家 扩散的故事。在技术部门内部，不积极编码的员工（定义为过去 30 天内没有代码提交的人）占比在截至 2026 年 4 月的一年里下降了近一半。部分原因是非工程师占比的减少：例如，工程师与产品经理的比例约为 17 比 1，且自 2025 年以来有所上升。管理者的提交次数也翻了一番。技术团队内部的监督和协调角色越来越多地涉及构建和交付代码。

blocks.text: 但有三项特征尤为突出。第一，广泛的股权持有使员工对公司的成功抱有强烈的利益关切。当然，对于一家估值大幅增长的公司来说，这是一种容易采取的立场。对许多公司而言，共享所有权可能并不充分，或者并不合意。但很难想象有一种支持工人的 AI 应用方式，其中工人却不在成功落地中持有财务利益。如果像受访者所说的那样，期望个人贡献者去“管理智能体”、“做出 VP 级别的决策”并成为“他们自己的业务线”，那么将他们的利益与组织对齐就至关重要。二战后于 1950 年代形成的工会与管理层和解，正是建立在这样一种交易之上：像美国汽车工人联合会和美国钢铁工人联合会这样的工会，允许管理层在工作重组（甚至工作强化）上拥有特权，以换取与生产率增长挂钩的加薪以及丰厚的一系列福利。无论受 AI 影响的员工与其雇主之间达成什么样的新协议，一种分享应用收益的机制都是必不可少的。在 Anthropic，工人们将自己的专业知识编纂给机器，眼看着自己的工作常规不断被搅动和打乱，并且看到自己工作的很大一部分变成了快速阅读其 AI 协作者的输出。他们做这些并不是免费的。

blocks.text: Key findings

inlines.text: Key findings

Anthropic has been hiring for a smaller share of junior technical positions. This occurred as hours worked by AI agents relative to employees rapidly expanded. By August interactive AI agent hours outnumbered employees’ 6 to 1.

As AI agents diffused through the company, Anthropic began producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts. Following the same employee over time, output rose as they adopted new AI tools.

This acceleration makes human attention the bottleneck for agent output. Even among non-technical employees, reading all the output of their Claude agents would take half their work week. In response, employees turn to “meta-work,” of building visibility tools and monitoring agent pipelines.
Changes in work organization are reflected in shifting priorities among hiring managers, who increasingly emphasize autonomy and judgment, relative to technical domain expertise and implementation.

blocks.text: What transformations of work and employment can we expect under increasingly powerful AI? Anthropic is worth studying because it has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI. Agents flit through Slack chats and schedule meetings. They autonomously fix bugs and collectively tackle huge engineering projects. Agent hours worked outnumber human hours 6 to 1. Changes happening at Anthropic now give advanced signals about a possible future of work and employment.

blocks.text: We find that even as the company grows, relative hiring in junior technical positions has slowed. Productivity for both engineers and non-technical employees has leapt up and did so sharply when they adopted coding agents. Hiring managers increasingly emphasize applicants’ autonomy and judgement relative to specific technical expertise. A defining feature of working in an AI-heavy organization is constant pressure to streamline oneself out of this bottleneck position when possible. One engineer described work as facing “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention.” Employees at Anthropic remain critical. But the nature of their contributions has changed.

blocks.text: At the same time, the overall employment share of technical departments within Anthropic has fallen, from 61% to 56% in the last year. As the company expands, technical hiring has continued growing in absolute terms, but intensive hiring in sales, finance, and recruiting has outpaced it. Part of this shift is the natural expansion of business functions as the company scales. Part could reflect coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves. For example, a sales representative designed a custom dashboard and pipeline tailored to their work: “a build like this was out of my wheelhouse, especially with the UI, connecting all the tools, the MCPs. blocks.text: Heavy AI adoption reshapes more than employment and productivity. It also drives continual changes in work processes, generating new tasks and shifting employees’ perceptions of their workplace. One employee described this as the “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything” and another that “things we expect in a week are things that would take three months elsewhere.” An internal employee survey asked whether work processes at Anthropic made respondents as productive as possible: 44% of employees agreed in late 2024; 58% by November 2025 (in April 2026, 75% answered yes, but the question weakened by dropping “as possible”). As of August, employees at Anthropic expected that AI will be able to do 75% of their work by 2030, compared to 28% for other Americans.

blocks.text: As humans work amid a growing fleet of AI agents, they face pressure to shift human work into agent-visible channels. If a decision is made in an in-person meeting, and no notes or report-out appears, agents are missing crucial context for updating their goals and assumptions. An employee explained how having their name on a months-old document about Claude swag meant agents kept bringing requests for t-shirts and mugs, long after their responsibilities had changed. Private work, in unlogged meetings and direct messages, is invisible, confusing and discouraged in an AI-heavy workplace. One researcher described this default toward openness as critical to Anthropic’s thoroughgoing integration of AI: “most organizations do not run that way and I think that's a big shift because leaders have to defend feedback out in the open.” The need to feed AI context requires observability of human work and decisions.

We used an automated coder to process hiring manager interview score cards for thousands of employees hired at Anthropic since 2024. blocks.text: The deep adoption of AI at Anthropic makes it a useful case. As AI diffuses and improves, the organization of work could shift as it has in prior waves of technological change. The railroads gave us the managerial corporation, steam power allowed factories, and personal computers delivered the startup. What new organizations will tool-using, reasoning LLMs require, and what will be our role in them? One possibility is single-person start-ups, each with a human founder steering swarms of agents to rake in billions in revenue. blocks.text: But three features stand out. First, widespread stock ownership gives employees a strong interest in the company’s success. Of course, this is an easy posture for a company that has seen substantial increases in valuation. For many firms, shared ownership may be insufficient or otherwise undesirable. But it is difficult to imagine a version of pro-worker AI adoption in which workers do not hold a financial stake in successful rollout. If individual contributors are expected to “manage agents,” “make VP level decisions” and be “their own business line,” as interviewees put it, then aligning their interests with the organization is crucial. The post-World War II union-management settlement forged in the 1950s rested on exactly this kind of bargain: labor unions like the United Auto Workers and the United Steel Workers allowed management prerogative over work reorganization (and even intensification) in return for pay increases tied to productivity increases and to a rich array of benefits. Whatever the new deal between AI-affected employees and their employers, a mechanism to share benefits of adoption is essential. At Anthropic, workers codify their expertise for the machine, see their work routines constantly roiled and disrupted, and have seen a large part of their job become speedreading the output of their AI collaborators. They do not do this for free.

blocks.text: Second, Anthropic is standing up an ongoing early warning system to monitor jobs facing AI-driven transformation. A series of role-level metrics for demand and productivity are read against AI capabilities and use. These aggregate metrics help flag where work is shifting. An early warning system allows the company to start reallocating affected employees to jobs with a skills fit that may be less immediately at risk. As companies across the economy reorient to an accelerated pace of work reorganization, effective systems for guiding internal employee reallocation will become increasingly valuable. Turning to the external labor market to meet every new task demanded by AI advances will be a stronger bottleneck the faster AI advances. In this report, we found increased mobility between departments, changing work content, and employees shifting to new tasks as old ones were automated. Building systems to flexibly reallocate workers internally will be critical for AI-intensive organizations.

blocks.text: This commitment to internal worker reallocation raises important tradeoffs. A well-functioning labor market should shift workers into their most productive positions, whether that is at their current employer or another one. Commitments to reallocate incumbent workers could make employers hesitant to take a risk on hiring new employees. In normal economic conditions, particularly intensely competitive ones, such commitments could be costly.
